name: Pure Polynucleotide (PDRN)

card.summary: Injectable salmon-DNA-derived 'skin booster' borrowed from wound-care medicine; promising lab and orthopaedic data, but little controlled evidence for facial appearance.
card.aka: PDRN, polydeoxyribonucleotide, salmon DNA, polynucleotide booster
card.note: Most human trials concern wounds and tendons, not cosmetic outcomes; injectable procedure performed by clinicians.

quick.overview:
PDRN, short for polydeoxyribonucleotide, is a mixture of DNA fragments, today mostly purified from salmon or trout reproductive tissue. It was first used in medicine for wound and tissue repair and is now marketed in several countries as an intradermal 'skin booster' meant to improve skin quality, scars and fine lines.

In appearance circles it is discussed as a regenerative alternative or add-on to hyaluronic acid boosters. Published human trials so far mostly cover wounds, tendons and joints, with cosmetic trials only recently registered.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory work indicates PDRN is broken down into components including adenosine, which acts on the A2A receptor and is linked to increased blood-vessel growth and tissue repair signalling. Proponents say this translates into better skin quality; this has not been established in large controlled facial trials.
quick.risks: Reported adverse effects in the trials surveyed are generally minor, and purified products are described as having low immunogenicity. Regulatory status varies by country and product (medicine in some, device or cosmetic in others). Injection-site reactions and the usual risks of intradermal procedures apply.

lead: Polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN) is a mixture of single-stranded DNA fragments that was first isolated from human placenta for pharmaceutical use in Italy and is now mainly purified from salmon or trout sperm.[1] It is used in wound-healing and tissue-repair medicine and, particularly in parts of Asia and Europe, as an injected cosmetic 'skin booster' marketed for skin quality, scars and aging signs.[1]

Laboratory research describes PDRN as acting through adenosine A2A receptor signalling, with effects on angiogenesis and inflammation.[1][2] Human trials have studied it mainly for diabetic ulcers, tendon problems and osteoarthritis rather than facial appearance.[3][4][5][6] Cosmetic studies, including scar and periocular wrinkle trials, are registered but small and recent.[7][8]
In looksmaxxing and aesthetic-procedure discussion it appears as a 'salmon DNA' or polynucleotide option alongside hyaluronic acid boosters.
infobox: Purified salmon or trout DNA; originally human placenta[1]

paras: PDRN is a polyanionic, water-soluble mixture of DNA fragments of widely varying size. Its biological activity is said to depend on the source and molecular weight, and highly purified products are described as lowering the chance of immune reactions.[1]
Commercial 'polynucleotide' gels used as skin boosters are related but distinct products with their own concentrations and device or cosmetic classifications.

Practitioners offer PDRN-based injections for skin texture, photoaging, scars and mottled pigmentation, and sometimes after lasers or microneedling.[1][4] A laboratory study reported that PDRN reduced melanin-related activity in cultured cells, and noted that some patients receiving PDRN injections reported improvement of photoaging-related mottled pigmentation.[4]
A small study combined platelet-rich plasma with PDRN injections around hair follicles in women with pattern hair loss.[9]

PDRN has been used for chronic wounds including diabetic foot ulcers, and for tendinopathy and osteoarthritis.[1][10] A registered phase 4 trial studied a placenta-derived PDRN product for diabetic ulcers.[11]

PDRN is reported to be broken down enzymatically, with adenosine activating the A2A receptor, raising cAMP and influencing pathways involved in angiogenesis such as VEGF, and supplying nucleotides to salvage pathways.[1] In genetically diabetic mice, PDRN treatment was reported to stimulate angiogenesis and wound healing, with A2 purinergic receptor involvement.[2]

Evidence on appearance outcomes is limited. A study in 20 women with female pattern hair loss, combining one platelet-rich plasma session with twelve weekly PDRN injections. Its outcomes are reported in the published paper.[9]

Randomised trials in other conditions include a saline-controlled trial in chronic plantar fasciitis and a comparison with corticosteroid injection in the same condition.[3][6] A retrospective comparative study examined supraspinatus tendinopathy,[5] and a meta-analysis of randomised trials evaluated knee osteoarthritis.[10] Animal studies have examined tendon injuries.[12][13][14]

Registered cosmetic trials include PDRN for post-operative scars (completed, n=22),[15] periocular wrinkles,[7] rolling acne scars compared with non-crosslinked hyaluronic acid,[16] and facial scars with fractional CO2 laser.[8] Results of these were not available in the sources reviewed.

The wound-healing mouse study described PDRN as having no toxic or adverse effect.[2] Reviews describe highly purified material as minimising immunological side effects,[1] although human cosmetic safety data remain limited to small studies. As with other injections, local reactions can occur.

PDRN has been popular in South Korea's dermatology market, where Wikipedia describes it as a common biostimulator after procedures such as laser or microneedling.[1] The term 'salmon DNA facial' has appeared in social media and press coverage; its community discussion is not documented in detail here.

timeline.event: Study in diabetic mice reports PDRN promoted wound healing and angiogenesis.[2]
Studies of PDRN in hair loss and plantar fasciitis published.[9][3]
Laboratory study of PDRN and melanin production published.[4]
Meta-analysis of PDRN for knee osteoarthritis published.[10]

lore.intro: Discussion of PDRN is mostly in clinic marketing and aesthetic-medicine channels, where it is presented as 'regenerative'. Forum material was not available for this entry.

claims.claim: PDRN regenerates skin and improves texture beyond hyaluronic acid boosters
claims.believers: Practitioners and clinics promoting it say the DNA fragments stimulate repair and fibroblast activity, so skin quality improves rather than just being hydrated.[1]
claims.experts: Mechanistic and animal data support tissue-repair effects,[2] but controlled human trials of facial skin quality are limited and recently registered.[7][16]

claims.believers: Proponents use it after lasers and for acne scars on the basis of its wound-healing record.[1]
claims.experts: Scar trials are registered, including a completed phase 4 study, but published results were not located.[15][16]

claims.claim: PDRN is a safe, non-immunogenic salmon product
claims.believers: Sellers say purification removes proteins that would trigger reactions.[1]
claims.experts: Animal data reported no toxicity,[2] and purified preparations are described as low-risk,[1] but long-term cosmetic safety data are limited.
